title: The Widows of Mathura Weep
subtitle: Kamsa's funeral rites are performed
story:
In the arena, the bodies of Kamsa and his brothers still lay where they had fallen, and the men of Mathura stood stunned among them. The day had begun as a festival of arms; it had ended with the king dead by the hand of a cowherd boy from across the river, and his brothers dead beside him. But already another sound was rising over the field, thin at first and then everywhere at once — the weeping of women.

The wives of the men who had died had found their husbands where they lay. They knelt in the dust and gathered the still bodies into their arms, and their cries rose together and tangled in the air. They called to the fallen by every name love keeps for the dead — lord, beloved, knower of righteousness, kind to the shelterless — and asked the question that all such grief asks: who will protect this city now that you are gone? Not all the men who died that day had been loved, but all of them were mourned. Even the widows of Kamsa wept, and the sound of it reached the palace and the streets.

Krishna did not turn away from the grief he had caused. He walked among the royal women and comforted them, and his gentleness there was the same hand that had broken the great bow and struck the king down. He had the customary funeral rites prepared for all the dead, so that no wife would be left to burn her husband's pyre without honor.

Then Ugrasena came to him — Kamsa's father, the old king. He approached burning with grief for his son, breathing like a man who had drunk poison, and before the gathered Yadavas, the great family to which he and Krishna both belonged, he reproached himself aloud. "By my childish folly and my anger," he said, "I have made widows of these thousand women. They bewail their husbands so piteously that even the lord of the dead would pity them. And yet — Kamsa was sinful, hated by the righteous, ruthless of temper. Death is better than such a life, and what pity should there be for him? The wicked are bound by death to reap their fruits; the good reach a blessed end." Then he made his request. "Let me perform the after-death rites of my son. Let me build his pyre, put fire to it, and offer the water-oblation, and so discharge my debt to him. After that, with my wife and daughters-in-law, I will live out my days in the forest among the animals. This is my only prayer."

Krishna heard him out, and surprise — and something like tenderness — softened his answer. "What you have said befits your age, your family, and your nature. But the inevitable work is done; why speak as if it were not? Though dead, Kamsa will receive funeral honors befitting a king. You are born of a great race and know everything that should be known; understand that destiny is inevitable." He did not refuse the old king the rites he asked for.

So they placed Kamsa's body in a palanquin, as the ritual law required, and carried it through the city to the northern bank of the Yamuna. There they raised the pyre, set the fire, and performed the rites for the dead king while the smoke rose slow over the river. The widows' mourning went on into the evening, until grief had worn itself thin enough to let the city begin its long work of living again.

The day that had begun with a wrestling match had ended with a funeral by the river. Mathura had won its freedom, but even freedom must bury its dead before it can be lived in.
reflection: The episode is grief without vengeance: the man who slew Kamsa comforts the widows and sees that the funeral rites are done, and even the king who hunted him for years is buried with the honors of a king. Krishna's power over the city is shown not in what he takes but in how he lets it mourn.
tradition_note: The Bhagavata keeps this episode brief; the Harivamsha expands it into a long exchange in which Ugrasena reproaches himself for his son's death and begs Krishna's leave for the funeral rites. This story follows both, keeping the Bhagavata's shape and the Harivamsha's detail.
next_story_tease: The pyre had barely cooled when the brothers turned toward the prison where their own parents still lay in bonds.
